source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: Greetings students and welcome to a 4-part series on adrenal gland pathology. This first video is an overview that provides a limited physiologic and pathologic framework for understanding adrenal disease. The clinical and laboratory analysis of adrenal disease can be challenging because of the system complexity and the physiologic consequences of too little or too much hormone.

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: These are the learning objectives for this session. The essential diseases center on hyperfunction or hypofunction of the layers or zones of the adrenal gland. So we'll talk about excess cortisol, too little cortisol, excess aldosterone or too little aldosterone, and enzyme abnormalities that result in virulizing syndromes. The remaining disease category is adrenal gland tumors, which can be functional or nonfunctional. Functional means they secrete unregulated amounts of hormone. All of these problems are expressed clinically.

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: This is a four part series. This recording is an overview. The second covers hyperfunction of the cortex. The third covers hypofunction of the cortex. The last recording summarizes tumors of the cortex and medulla and some of the multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes that include adrenal medullary tumors.

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: This slide shows the synthetic pathways in each zone of the adrenal cortex. While you don't need to memorize intermediates, it is important to recognize some of the enzymes, particularly 21-hydroxylase. Deficiency of that enzyme is an important cause of adrenal hyperplasia and a virulizing syndrome that I'll discuss in the second recording.

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: The adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine. This is the synthetic pathway for that compound, but intermediates are also important neurotransmitters. The most significant disease of the adrenal medulla is pheochromocytoma, a tumor that can be productive for catecholamines. The tumor is often associated with intractable hypertension.

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: You should also realize that secretion of cortisol varies during the day. This concept is actually very important in the interpretation of laboratory measurements of cortisol and ACTH. It is also critical to realize that while laboratory values may be within the reference range, loss of the diurnal cycling is a clinically significant finding.

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: The laboratory testing of the adrenal gland is based on the physiologic regulation of that gland. So, this testing involves consideration of pituitary hormones produced by the pituitary or produced by some other neuroendocrine tumor. The testing involves glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and many regulated analytes altered by these hormones. All of these tests can be used to evaluate adrenal function. The choice of testing depends to a large degree on the clinical presentation. I'll cover this testing in the second and third recording.

source: Adrenal Gland Pathology Segment 1 - Overview accompanying
context: Adrenal gland disease falls into three big categories. They are hyperfunction, hypofunction and neoplasia. The clinical presentation depends entirely on what hormones are in excess or deficient and co-morbidities that may be operating. By the end of the series, you'll have some familiarity with these clinical problems.
